A putting green on a Southchase lawn, not a golf lot

A backyard putting green in Southchase runs $14–$30 a square foot installed, typically $18–$25, as of September 2026. Southchase doesn't sit on a golf course the way some newer Central Florida communities do, so a green here usually competes for space with a screened pool cage and a fenced yard rather than sitting on an oversized fairway lot.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Building a green where the lot wasn't drawn for one

Southchase's subdivisions were platted as suburban single-family and patio-home blocks, not around a golf amenity, so a putting green here almost always shares a modest backyard with a pool cage, a shed or a play area rather than sitting alone on a half-acre fairway lot. That changes the design brief: instead of a sprawling multi-hole layout, most Southchase greens are a single contoured pad, sized to what's left after the pool deck and a side setback are subtracted, with a fringe collar doing double duty as the rest of the lawn.

Contouring on soil that already sheds water

The sandy flatwoods base under Southchase actually helps a putting green's foundation, since the same washed crushed rock that keeps a lawn from ponding also holds a shaped contour better than a soft, organic-rich soil would. Building the subtle breaks and tiers a true roll needs takes more shaping labor on a small urban lot than on open ground, because there's less room to blend a slope into the surrounding grade before it hits a fence line or a patio edge.

Shaping a base that holds its breaks

A putting green's base in Southchase is a smaller, more deliberate version of a lawn base, hand-shaped into the designed slopes and tiers rather than screeded flat like the rest of the yard. Washed, open-graded crushed rock or crushed concrete still goes down two to four inches deep in compacted lifts, but each lift gets shaped to the break plan before the next one starts, since correcting a slope after the surface is bonded down is far harder than getting it right in the rock. A green that loses its shape within a season almost always started with a base that was compacted flat and shaped only at the very top layer.

Setting cups once the base is fully shaped

Cups go in after the Southchase green's base has been shaped, compacted, and confirmed to hold its breaks, cored through at the design's marked locations rather than positioned by eye during installation. Each cup gets set and edged individually, which takes longer per hole than any other single step in building a green, since a slightly crooked or poorly seated cup stands out immediately against a surface built for precision. Waiting until the base is finished before coring also avoids having to patch a cup location that turns out to sit in the wrong spot once the shape is complete.

Say you have a side yard in Arlington Park

Say you have a side yard in Arlington Park, 500 sq ft between the pool cage and the fence, currently dead St. Augustine that never got enough sun to hold. At the published putting range of $14–$30 a square foot, a single contoured green with a fringe collar and two cups prices between $7,000 and $15,000, with most jobs landing in the typical $18–$25 band, or $9,000 to $12,500. A tighter footprint like this one usually pushes toward the top of that range, since contouring and fringe work don't shrink proportionally just because the pad is smaller.

What the putting green price range includes

Backyard putting green installation runs fourteen to thirty dollars a square foot, typically eighteen to twenty-five, well above a plain lawn's range because the base is hand-shaped rather than screeded flat and the surface product itself is chosen for ball roll instead of appearance. A Southchase homeowner comparing a lawn quote to a green quote for the same square footage should expect that difference to show up in labor and shaping time as much as in the turf product, since contouring a base to hold breaks takes longer than compacting one flat ever does.

Fitting a green around a pool cage instead of a fairway

Where a Southchase lot already has a screened pool enclosure, which is the norm on the single-family side of the community, a putting green usually ends up in the strip between the cage and the back fence, or wrapped around the cage's outside edge. That layout puts the green closer to a shared property line than a golf-community green would sit, which is one more reason a fenced-yard green rarely runs into visibility concerns under an HOA's exterior rules the way a front-yard installation would.

Drip lines and a shaded green under mature oaks

The same drip-line rule that keeps turf away from a live oak's roots applies to a putting green, and a shaded spot under mature canopy that looks appealing for a Southchase green during the hottest months still requires a certified arborist's sign-off before any shaping or excavation happens nearby. Excavating four to six inches for a green's base is deeper than a lawn conversion, which makes root damage a bigger risk under canopy than it would be for grass alone. Choosing a different, sunnier spot for the green and keeping the shaded area as fringe or lawn instead is often the simpler path.

Clearing debris from a green's low tiers

Leaves and pine needles collect fastest in a Southchase green's low tiers, the same spots already doing the most drainage work, and letting debris sit there breaks it down into the infill and can slow water movement exactly where the base needs to move it fastest. Clearing those low spots promptly after they accumulate, rather than waiting for a general yard cleanup, keeps both the roll and the drainage performing as designed. A green with several tiers takes a few extra minutes to check compared with a flat lawn, since debris doesn't distribute evenly across a shaped surface.

Questions people ask

Does Southchase have a golf community with putting green amenities built in?

No. Southchase is a suburban single-family and patio-home community without a golf course, so a putting green here is a standalone backyard build rather than an extension of an existing course.

Can a Southchase putting green share space with a pool cage?

Yes, and it's the common layout here; the green typically runs along the outside of the screen enclosure or in the strip left over after the cage and setbacks are subtracted from the lot.
